lines.note: A horse or folding screens exemplify the identical borrowed objects returned under henshin on the preceding page, unlike fungible rice or money.

lines.note: The Portuguese describes illuminating everything, attributed to non-Christian belief. Tudo corrects the OCR tado without endorsing the source's religious framing.
Fotoque completes the statement that the Buddha illuminates all things. It is embedded Japanese in the Portuguese sentence.
Another henshou is reversing the palm, tanagokoro wo kaesu, used to explain rapid change rather than Buddhist illumination.

lines.note: The comparison is turning the palm of the hand, emphasizing the ease or speed of reversal.

lines.note: Henshu is speaking ill of or scorning something. The headword's F and n restore the OCR Beuxu corruption.

Henyaku, te uchi odoru, is dancing while clapping. This paired Japanese explanation supports the F initial.

lines.note: The clapping is an expression of joy; bailar completes the divided Portuguese verb.

Completes variedade: change and variation are the Portuguese gloss pair.
Henyet, te uchi yorokobu, is rejoicing by clapping. Final t is a checked coda; Alegrar-se contains long s, not f.
As palmas completes the clapping description, not a separate entry or example.

runs.text: Nome de hum animal como on-

lines.note: Hyou, written Feo or fio, denotes a leopard-like animal, compared with onca. This entry then turns into an important spelling explanation.
The authors say they ordinarily write these words with e. Here e is a cited Latin letter, not Japanese running text.

lines.note: The explanation concerns words whose Japanese written forms begin or end in the sequence specified next; comecao and acabao form a pair.

lines.note: Eu is the cited spelling sequence. Pronunciation is contrasted with spelling; pronunci ar was an OCR consonant error, not a historical phonetic term.
The pronunciation approaches i more than e. These isolated letters are metalinguistic examples, so kana hints for them are not lexical readings.

runs.text: os do Cami tambem aſſi pronucião.

lines.note: Fio supplies the example, and the authors say Cami speakers also pronounce it that way. The t-like OCR letter is dotted i.

lines.note: The reader is referred to the prologue for a fuller account of this spelling/pronunciation relationship.
Te razao completes 'a fuller explanation'. This short row closes the dictionary's orthographic digression.
A separate hyou, glossed tawara, means a bale. It is not the animal discussed in the preceding long entry.
Hyouban is consultation or deliberation, with dankou suru as its Japanese explanation. Preserve the source's marks individually.
Consulta completes fazer consulta, giving the deliberative sense rather than modern reputation.

lines.note: Hyouhaku is drifting or stopping while adrift. The alternative fio spelling includes i, which OCR omitted.
Kanata konata e yuraruru describes movement to and fro. Fluctuando begins the Portuguese account of floating or wandering.

lines.note: The movement is from here to there, or a vessel being detained; the sentence's subject is supplied below.

runs.text: a embarcação por varios portos cõ ruim tempo.

lines.note: Bad weather keeps the vessel at various ports. This completes the maritime explanation of hyouhaku.
Per met. introduces a figurative use: wandering through different places, no longer specifically by ship.

runs.text: partes como ganhando ſua vida ſem ter lugar

lines.note: The wanderer makes a living without a fixed place. The adjective certo is separated onto the next row.
Certo completes lugar certo: a settled or fixed location is lacking.
Hyouhou is fencing, with a cross-reference to the fio spelling. The nasal-looking OCR mark is a vowel-length mark in that reference.
Hyouhoye refers to a mounted image or painting. The Portuguese begins the description of its mounting materials.

runs.text: certa guarnição de ſeda, ou papel, &c.

lines.note: Silk, paper, and similar materials furnish the mounting; this helps connect the term with the following hyougu entry.
Hyoufu, 'ice skin', describes a pale complexion. The Japanese explanation is koori, hadae, rather than literal bodily ice.
Carne muito alvo completes the explanation of very white flesh or complexion.
Hyougaku concerns hides or leather; the military application follows. Initial C in OCR was the damaged F seen in neighboring entries.

runs.text: que cobrem na China os carros que leuão na guer

lines.note: The hides cover Chinese vehicles used in war. Guerra is divided across the next row.

runs.text: ra. ¶ Item, Guerra que ſe aleuanta.

lines.note: After completing guerra, Item adds the further sense of war breaking out.
Hyouge mono or hyougeta mono denotes an unusual or eccentric person. Initial Ee was OCR noise around F.
Singular e extravagante supplies the character description; the cross-reference uses the alternative fio spelling.
Mono completes the cross-referenced hyouge mono. It is not a new independent headword.
Hyoujou, explained as dankou, is consultation. The following homophone has a different military sense.
The second hyoujou means weapons such as a spear or sword. Do not merge it with the preceding deliberation entry.
Hyougu has the same weapon sense as the final entry in column 1. Idem crosses the column boundary in reference, not in physical text.
Another hyougu is equipment or material for mounting pictures. The gloss begins a list of cloth pieces and similar materials.

runs.text: de peça, &c. pera o ornato das imagens, ou-

lines.note: These materials ornament images or paintings. The printed line-end sign after ou is retained even though it is not a lexical split.
Pinturas completes the second object of the mounting, alongside imagens.
Hyouji, hioshigoto, is a likeness or preliminary representation of something. The interpretation is not simply modern display.

runs.text: figura dalgũa couſa que ſe ha de fazer. ¶

lines.note: The likeness represents what is going to be made. Fio at the end begins a repeated equivalent term below.
Completes fio-ji and gives feozou as an equivalent, marked S. The initial is j, not long s.
A homophonous hyouji means soldiers, explained by tsuwamono otoko. The OCR space within soldados is retained pending precise typography review.
Hyoumot, tawara mono, means bales. Final t belongs to the checked ending rather than an omitted tsu syllable.
Rice and wheat are the contents of the bales. Kura ni hyoumot wo begins the example of storing them.
Voſame voqu gives osame oku, storing away the bundles. Enlargement supports lowercase vo at the beginning rather than the OCR's Vu; the following Portuguese means putting the goods into storage.
The Portuguese says storing bales of rice and wheat in a house or store, confirming the preceding object.

lines.note: Hyouki, setsukotsu evokes delicate skin and bones, glossed utsukushii hadae. The isolated final t spellings are checked syllables.

lines.note: The expression describes a very delicate body or limbs, and is marked as written usage.
Hyouri directs the reader to Fiori and fiorimono. Restore F rather than OCR B without expanding the cross-reference into a new definition.

lines.note: Hyourin, 'ice wheel', is glossed tsuki, the moon. Tcuqi is the tsuki spelling, not OCR Fcuqi.
Lua is the Portuguese moon gloss, followed by S. The whole short row had been mistaken for Japanese sua and needed its typeface restored.
Hyouso denotes a disease of the hands. The following row specifies finger swelling and a regional synonym.
The fingers swell, and Ximo calls it motobu. Ximo and Motobu are Japanese terms inside the Portuguese explanation.
Hyoutan denotes gourds. The paired feo/fio spellings are retained without normalizing their separately printed vowel marks.
Hyoutei, koori no soko, is beneath the ice. Caramelo below is the historical Portuguese ice term, not confectionery.
Hyoutei ni uo kurushimu describes fish suffering beneath ice. The generated kana may misleadingly read vuo as a particle; here it is the fish noun.

runs.text: O peixe padece tormẽto de baxo do caramelo.

lines.note: The fish suffers torment beneath the ice. Tormẽto restores the printed nasal abbreviation rather than inserting a full n.

lines.note: Hyoutokugou is a name expressing virtue or quality. Toku wo arawasu begins the Japanese explanation and exposes OCR's To uuo segmentation.

runs.text: Nome que declara a virtude, & qua

lines.note: Completes arawasu na, a name that expresses virtue. Virtude is the Portuguese counterpart; OCR had substituted i for t.
Qualidade da cousa completes the defining quality of the named thing.
Hyouset, koori/yuki, is ice and snow. The fio alternative starts with f, not long s; both the sense and printed form agree.
Hyouset imada kiyezu means the ice and snow have not yet disappeared or melted. Qiyezu corrects OCR quyezu.

runs.text: Ainda ſe não deſfez o caramelo, & a neue.

lines.note: The Portuguese says the ice and snow have not yet dissolved. Desfez contains long s followed by f, not double f.

runs.text: Feôxet, l, fiôxet. i, Yuqiuo furu tei.

lines.note: Another hyouset describes the manner of snow falling. The Japanese form is retained as printed even if its particle seems unexpected.

runs.text: do de chouer neue que ſe parece com roſas que

lines.note: The falling snow is compared with roses or flowers scattering; this is a descriptive literary image.
Se espalhao completes the scattering comparison, not an independent predicate about the dictionary entry.
Hyoushi denotes bells or jingles. Cascaveis restores the missing final s at the right edge while retaining Cumpainhas as printed.

runs.text: que poem nos caualos de carga.

lines.note: The bells are attached to pack horses; this identifies the practical equipment sense of hyoushi.
A separate hyoushi is a cover or binding. Encadernacao is divided between rows.

runs.text: ção de papel, que fazem nos liuros da China,

lines.note: The binding is made of paper for Chinese books; Japanese books are included in the continuation.
Iapao closes the geographical pair. Hyoushi wo suru / kakuru introduces alternative verbs for putting on the cover.
Kisuru is a further covering verb, not OCR qisuiu. The Portuguese begins making this cover or binding.
Completes encadernacao, closing the book-cover example.
Another hyoushi is musical meter or rhythm. Instrumentos continues across the following row.
Hyoushi ga sorou or ou describes agreement in rhythm. The printed vowel marks are retained rather than chosen from modern spelling.
The music proceeds in order and in time. A contrasting example begins with another divided hyoushi.
Hyoushi ga chigou or sorowanu means failing to agree in rhythm. Discrepar corrects the OCR vowel in the Portuguese verb.
Desentoar explains being out of tune or time. Hyoushi ni kakatte introduces dancing in relation to the beat; the doubled t is visible.
Mou or odoru supplies two dancing verbs, with the Portuguese tomar phrase continuing below.

runs.text: mando o tom da muſica, ou do inſtrumento

lines.note: The dancer follows the music or instrument's tone or beat. This completes the sense of kakatte in the example.
Musico completes instrumento musico. The separate Feo catchword is page furniture rather than part of this final body row.
